I think it's more a case of the education of software consumers game gradually and with much complaining.

The same laws that govern the ownership of books basically govern the ownership of software. When you buy a book, you own the physical media. You own the covers, the pages, and the ink, but you don't own the content. 20 years ago the application of software licensing was very different, because there wasn't really a way to track and/or revoke a license. Hence why people could buy games and think they owned them...there was nothing slapping them about the head reminding them that they don't. The licensing back then was more a legal clause the opened the door to prosecution if you were found to be duplicating and selling bootleg copies of the games.

Now we have DRM. And with that comes a more obvious indication to consumers that they paid for a license, not ownership of the IP. The terms of use haven't changed.

If you owned a game, that, by definition, would grant you the rights to do with it as you please, including the right to duplicate and sell it to your hearts content.

You've never owned a game. All you've ever had was a license to play it. We need to keep this distinction clear.

I agree to a point, especially about lack of education - I'd say it's more about apathy about licensing rules that weren't rigorously enforced before. No one cares if you legally own the software if you practically do, and that's been enough for most people up to a point. The big shift lately is that with cloud software, more pervasive DRM, and games that rely on constant updates and an active internet connection to function, we're losing that practical control as well.

I may not have the legal ability to make copies of book or game, but I can loan the book to a friend who wants to read it, or give it away/sell it if I decide to. I don't have copyright on the book, but I do own the book in a much more real sense than simply a license to read. Video games have had the "license to play" approach coming for some time now, it's just that now it's becoming easier to enforce and tougher to crack.

It wasn't about apathy about the rules before...it was about the practicality of enforcing them. DRM methodologies have improved dramatically in the last several years. Gone of the days of DRM that entrenches itself so deeply into your OS install that you need a third party app to get rid of it all. That's what gave DRM a bad name. People complaining about the DRM we see these days are just regurgitating what they heard about "DRM" in general. I'll take Steam's DRM over SecuROM any damn day of the week.

This thread is an extremely poignant example of someone suddenly becoming aware of the laws that have always governed the sale of software licenses and thinking that it's a recent phenomenon. It's not. That's really the bottom line. "Ignorance of the law is not an excuse." Doesn't matter if people are just learning about it now or why...the specifics have always been laid out in every ToS you've ever agreed to whether it came up when you first launched a game or was printed on the last pages of the manual that came with the disk.

So if it's always been there, we can't really complain about it like it hasn't always been there. (And for what it's worth, as the printed book loses ground to digital book distribution, publishers are taking advantage of the ability to protect their rights with DRM of their own.)
